paragraphs: ActAnywhere addresses the problem of generating a video background that fits a moving foreground subject. For film and visual effects work, this involves more than choosing scenery: the subject and surroundings need to appear to interact plausibly. The paper aims to automate a process that otherwise requires substantial manual effort.

The method uses a video diffusion model with two inputs: a sequence of foreground subject segmentations and an image specifying the desired background. Together, these describe the subject’s motion and the scene into which it should be placed. The model learns from 2.4 million videos of human interactions with scenes, giving it training examples of how foreground movement relates to surrounding environments.

The evaluations report realistic interactions while closely following the supplied background image. They also demonstrate generalization to non-human subjects, gaming and animation footage, and multiple moving subjects. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show substantial improvements over existing methods for this task. These findings support using subject motion as a central condition for generating coherent replacement backgrounds.
neurips-2024-actanywhere-subject-aware-v.tldr: ActAnywhere generates video backgrounds guided by a reference image and foreground motion to produce realistic subject–scene interactions.

paragraphs: A Decision Transformer learns actions from recorded trajectories while conditioning on a desired return. In adversarial environments, however, a high recorded return may reflect a weak opponent rather than a strong strategy. Learning to reproduce actions associated with that return can therefore fail when a more capable adversary appears.

The Adversarially Robust Decision Transformer changes the return used for learning and conditioning. It estimates in-sample minimax returns-to-go through minimax expectile regression, aligning the policy’s target with a learned worst-case outcome. The central idea is to account for the adversary when interpreting what the recorded trajectories say about the quality of an action.

In sequential-game experiments with full data coverage, ARDT can produce a maximin strategy, corresponding to a Nash equilibrium in the studied setting. With partial coverage in larger games and continuous adversarial reinforcement-learning environments, it achieves higher worst-case returns and stronger robustness than contemporary Decision Transformer methods. The full-coverage result and the partial-coverage empirical improvements are distinct: the latter demonstrate better performance without establishing the same equilibrium outcome.
neurips-2024-adversarially-robust-decisi.tldr: ARDT conditions action selection on learned worst-case returns to improve robustness against stronger adversaries.

paragraphs: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning trains a policy to imitate demonstrations using a reward supplied by an adversarial discriminator. The policy improves through on-policy reinforcement learning, but the resulting optimization can oscillate. Those oscillations can delay convergence and prevent the learner from reaching a good imitation policy.

The paper studies this interaction through control theory. Its analysis of GAIL’s training dynamics shows that GAIL cannot reach the desired equilibrium in the analyzed formulation. The authors then design a controller in function space that directs learning toward that equilibrium. They establish asymptotic stability for a simplified one-step setting, giving a theoretical basis for stabilizing the coupled learning process.

The practical method, Controlled-GAIL, adds a differentiable regularization term to the GAIL objective. Experiments show that this regularizer improves several existing GAIL methods, including GAIL-DAC, through faster convergence, smaller oscillations, and closer agreement with the expert distribution. The practical findings support the control-based design, while the formal stability result remains tied to the simplified setting in which it was established.
neurips-2024-c-gail-stabilizing-generati.tldr: C-GAIL uses a control-theoretic regularizer to reduce training oscillations and improve imitation learning.

paragraphs: DF40 asks whether success on familiar deepfake benchmarks translates into detecting the diversity of manipulated content encountered outside those benchmarks. The paper identifies the training and testing datasets as a possible primary source of the gap. Limited forgery coverage, older generation techniques, and evaluations restricted to one manipulation type can all give an incomplete picture of detector capability.

The authors construct a dataset covering 40 distinct deepfake techniques. Its broader coverage addresses a field that includes face swapping, face reenactment, and complete image synthesis, while many existing datasets represent only some of these categories. The aim is to test detection across a richer range of forgeries rather than rely on a narrow collection of familiar examples.

The benchmark evaluates eight representative detection methods under four standard protocols, producing more than 2,000 evaluations. The resulting analysis reports seven findings and four underexplored research questions. Its contribution is a broader foundation for assessing generalization: detector rankings become more informative when the underlying data and evaluation protocols reflect the variety of the detection problem.
neurips-2024-df40-toward-next-generation.tldr: DF40 broadens deepfake detection evaluation with 40 forgery techniques and an extensive comparison of representative detectors.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference in linear mixed-effects models often relies on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to sample from a model written in a probabilistic programming language. Yet mathematically related ways of expressing a model can lead to very different computational efficiency. A useful transformation is marginalization: accounting for some variables without asking the sampler to represent them explicitly.

This paper develops an algorithm for marginalizing random effects in these models. Doing that transformation manually is difficult, and a straightforward implementation introduces operations with cubic running time inside inference. The authors use fast linear algebra to reduce that computational cost to linear time, making the transformation more practical to incorporate into Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

The paper reports that marginalization is beneficial whenever the proposed approach is applicable, and demonstrates improvements across several models, particularly from cognitive science. The applicability condition matters: the claim concerns models where this marginalization can be used. The contribution combines an easier model transformation with efficient computation, addressing both the user effort and the runtime costs that can otherwise discourage marginalization.
neurips-2024-hamiltonian-monte-carlo-inf.tldr: The paper makes random-effect marginalization practical for applicable linear mixed-effects models by reducing its computational cost from cubic to linear.

paragraphs: Programming feedback systems need to provide useful hints, but classroom deployment also depends on cost, response time, and data privacy. This paper benchmarks language models across those criteria instead of judging them solely by how closely their feedback resembles that of a human tutor. It treats deployment requirements as part of the educational task.

The approach uses in-browser inference, allowing models to run directly within the browser. This offers direct cost and privacy benefits, while creating a need for smaller models that still generate good feedback. To improve their quality, the authors build a fine-tuning pipeline using synthetic training data generated by GPT-4.

The study demonstrates fine-tuned Llama3-8B and Phi3-3.8B models, both using 4-bit quantization, through WebLLM’s browser inference engine on three Python programming datasets. The results support the usefulness of adapting compact models for this setting. The contribution connects feedback quality with practical delivery constraints, showing how model training and local execution can be evaluated together when designing programming education tools.
neurips-2024-hints-in-browser-benchmarki.tldr: Hints-In-Browser evaluates locally running programming-feedback models across quality, cost, latency, and privacy, using synthetic-data fine-tuning to improve small models.

paragraphs: Shape matching seeks corresponding points on different shapes, but accuracy and smoothness can pull in different directions. A highly distinctive descriptor can identify an individual mesh vertex while behaving irregularly across nearby vertices or reacting poorly to noise. A smoother descriptor can preserve neighborhood continuity while losing the detail needed to distinguish exact points.

HOPE uses neighborhoods at different numbers of mesh hops as pairwise descriptors. These neighborhoods describe a vertex through surrounding mesh structure at several extents, rather than relying on a single kind of vertex signature. The method combines these descriptors with local map distortion to refine an already initialized correspondence map.

The authors validate the pipeline on shape-matching benchmarks including SCAPE, TOSCA, and TOPKIDS. The stated results support the effectiveness of using multiple neighborhood scales together with distortion information. The role of initialization is central to interpreting the method: HOPE improves an existing map. Its contribution is a refinement strategy aimed at reconciling precise point correspondence with the continuity expected of a smooth match.
neurips-2024-hope-shape-matching-via-ali.tldr: HOPE refines shape correspondences using multiple mesh-neighborhood scales and local distortion to address the tension between accuracy and smoothness.

paragraphs: Predicting how a protein mutation changes its effects is useful for protein engineering and biological understanding. Practical decisions also require knowing how much confidence to place in a prediction. The paper highlights an imbalance in this area: prediction accuracy has improved, while uncertainty quality is much less frequently reported.

Kermut is a Gaussian process regression model with a new composite kernel for expressing similarity between mutations. That similarity structure supports supervised prediction of protein variant effects. The model also provides uncertainty estimates through its posterior, placing the prediction and its uncertainty within the same modeling framework rather than assessing accuracy alone.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art predictive performance and find meaningful overall uncertainty calibration. However, calibration for individual instances remains more difficult. This distinction matters because uncertainty can behave sensibly across a collection of predictions without being equally informative for each specific variant. Kermut therefore contributes both a strong predictor and an explicit examination of how far its uncertainty estimates support the confidence judgments needed in protein engineering.
neurips-2024-kermut-composite-kernel-reg.tldr: Kermut combines strong protein variant prediction with posterior uncertainty estimates, achieving meaningful overall calibration while leaving instance-level calibration challenging.

paragraphs: A representation model can sometimes reveal information about a training image’s foreground even when given only its background. The déjà vu memorization test looks for predictive ability beyond what ordinary correlations in the dataset would explain. This distinction is essential: a background can legitimately correlate with a foreground category without implying that a particular training example was memorized.

Earlier measurement required training two models, one to estimate dataset correlations and another to estimate memorization. That makes the procedure impractical for large released models. This paper proposes simpler ways to estimate the correlation component, allowing memorization in an existing model to be approximated without retraining it.

The approach enables evaluation of pretrained open-source image representation and vision-language models. Different measurement methods produce very similar aggregate results, supporting the usefulness of the cheaper estimates at that level. The authors also find that open-source models typically exhibit less aggregate memorization than comparable models trained on a data subset. These are aggregate comparisons, rather than claims that every example or every released model behaves identically.
neurips-2024-measuring-dejavu-memorizati.tldr: The paper estimates déjà vu memorization in existing vision models without retraining by simplifying the measurement of dataset-level correlations.

paragraphs: Data balancing is often used to improve fairness or robustness by removing unwanted associations among inputs, outcomes, and other factors. The intended effect is straightforward: reduce dependencies that encourage undesirable predictions. This paper examines when modifying the training distribution in this way actually leads to the desired model behavior.

The authors define conditions on the training distribution under which balancing produces fair or robust models. Their analysis uses the task’s causal graph to distinguish the dependencies a balancing procedure changes from the dependencies one intends to remove. In many cases, the resulting balanced distribution does not correspond to selectively eliminating only the unwanted causal relationships.

That mismatch creates several failure modes and can interfere with other mitigation methods, including regularization. The result does not imply that balancing always fails; its value depends on how the distributional change relates to the causal structure of the task. The paper’s practical message is that balancing should be assessed through that structure, because changing observed associations alone may not accomplish the intended fairness or robustness intervention.
neurips-2024-mind-the-graph-when-balanci.tldr: Data balancing improves fairness or robustness only under appropriate conditions, and causal graphs help explain when it changes the wrong dependencies.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model involves decisions about hyperparameters and which checkpoint to retain. Model fusion offers another option by combining multiple models in parameter space. But choosing a good combination requires deciding what to optimize, and the paper observes a substantial mismatch between the training loss landscape and the landscape of the desired evaluation metric.

The proposed method uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization to guide model fusion while considering both loss and the target metric. This directly addresses the possibility that a combination favored by one objective may not be favored by the other. The authors also introduce a two-stage procedure that incorporates Bayesian optimization into hyperparameter selection.

Experiments across multiple downstream tasks report considerable performance improvements from the resulting framework. The contribution is an approach to selecting and combining fine-tuned models that explicitly recognizes the difference between a training objective and the outcome users evaluate. By coordinating fusion and hyperparameter selection, the method addresses two engineering choices that otherwise complicate finding an effective final model.
neurips-2024-model-fusion-through-bayesi.tldr: The paper uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization to fuse fine-tuned language models while jointly considering loss, target metrics, and hyperparameter selection.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce impressive scenes while struggling to render natural-looking faces and hands. MoLE addresses this problem through both training data and model adaptation. The paper attributes these weaknesses to insufficient training priors and seeks to provide more focused examples of human appearance at different scales.

The authors collect more than one million high-quality images of people in scenes, alongside separate close-up datasets for faces and hands. They then train low-rank modules on the close-up collections and treat those modules as specialized experts. This design follows their observation that a module trained on close-ups can improve the corresponding image region when applied at an appropriate scale.

Mixture of Low-rank Experts combines this specialized refinement with the broader human-centered data effort. The authors construct two benchmarks and evaluate the approach using multiple metrics and human studies to assess its advantages over state-of-the-art methods. The scale qualification is important: the proposed benefit depends on applying close-up expertise appropriately, rather than assuming that specialized training automatically improves every generated scene.
neurips-2024-mole-enhancing-human-centri.tldr: MoLE combines human-focused datasets with face and hand low-rank experts to improve human-centered image generation.

paragraphs: Expand-and-sparsify representations first randomly map a data point from a unit sphere into a higher-dimensional space. They then retain a small selection of coordinates as binary ones and set the rest to zero. This paper develops two non-parametric classifiers built from that sparse representation and studies when they learn at optimal rates.

The first classifier uses winners-take-all sparsification. The authors show that it can be expressed as a locally weighted average classifier and establish consistency using Stone’s Theorem. Under a Hölder continuity assumption on the conditional class probability, and with an optimal choice of expanded dimension, they additionally establish a minimax-optimal convergence rate.

The second classifier uses empirical k-thresholding. Assuming the data lie on a low-dimensional manifold, its convergence rate depends on the manifold dimension rather than the larger ambient dimension, and is again minimax-optimal. Evaluations on real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The significance is conditional but substantial: these simple sparse representations can support statistically optimal classification under the respective smoothness, dimension-selection, and manifold assumptions.
neurips-2024-non-parametric-classificati.tldr: Two expand-and-sparsify classifiers achieve minimax-optimal convergence under their stated smoothness and low-dimensional structure assumptions.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models requires substantial memory for gradient computation. This paper explores transferring expertise from task-specific smaller models to a larger model without additional training of the larger model. It operates through logit arithmetic, combining the scores used during generation to bring specialized knowledge into the larger model’s decisions.

The proposed method uses several small specialists and adjusts their weights at each decoding step. Those weights are learned through optimization constrained by Kullback-Leibler divergence. This dynamic allocation addresses two shortcomings identified in existing approaches: a fixed transfer ratio and dependence on a single small model to supply complex expertise.

In experiments transferring expertise from 7B to 13B models, the method closes 96.4% of the performance gap to full 13B fine-tuning in single-task settings and 86.3% in multi-task settings. These figures describe gap closure, not absolute accuracy. The paper also reports superior performance on unseen tasks and demonstrates compatibility with in-context learning and task arithmetic. Together, the findings support adjusting the contribution of specialists throughout generation.
neurips-2024-on-giant-s-shoulders-effort.tldr: Dynamic logit fusion transfers expertise from multiple small specialists to a larger model by adapting their contributions at each generation step.

paragraphs: Aligned language models can still be induced to generate harmful content through manually designed or optimized adversarial prompts. IBProtector introduces a defense at the prompt-processing stage. Its aim is to preserve the information needed for an appropriate answer while reducing the influence of prompt content that enables a jailbreak.

The method draws on the information bottleneck principle and modifies its objective to avoid trivial solutions. A lightweight trainable extractor selectively compresses and perturbs the prompt before it reaches the target model. The paper also considers a setting where target-model gradients are unavailable, extending the approach to models that do not expose those internal signals.

Empirical evaluations report stronger jailbreak mitigation than current defense methods without excessive effects on response quality or inference speed. Results across multiple attacks and target models support the approach’s transferability. The contribution is a defense that can operate without modifying the underlying language model, with the reported security and utility balance established through the evaluated settings rather than a universal guarantee against attacks.
neurips-2024-protecting-your-llms-with-i.tldr: IBProtector compresses and perturbs prompts to reduce jailbreak success while preserving useful responses without modifying the target model.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle when new graphs differ substantially from those encountered during training. RAGraph addresses this generalization problem by bringing external graph examples into a graph foundation model during inference. The model can thereby use relevant retrieved information as context for the task it is currently solving.

The framework builds a vector library of toy graphs containing attributes such as features and task-specific label information. At inference time, it retrieves graphs based on similarities relevant to the downstream task. A message-passing prompting mechanism incorporates those examples, connecting retrieval to the relational processing used by the graph model.

Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art graph learning methods on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification, covering static and dynamic datasets. Additional testing finds consistently high performance without task-specific fine-tuning. These results support retrieval as a means of adapting graph predictions to new scenarios: useful external structure and labels can enrich the model’s context without requiring a separate fine-tuning procedure for each evaluated task.
neurips-2024-ragraph-a-general-retrieval.tldr: RAGraph retrieves relevant external graph examples during inference to improve generalization across graph tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.

paragraphs: RePAIR provides a benchmark for reconstructing genuinely broken objects using fragments of a fresco that collapsed during a World War II bombing at Pompeii. Its pieces have irregular shapes and sizes, erosion, and missing material. These properties make the reconstruction task substantially different from simplified synthetic puzzles with clean, complete pieces.

The dataset combines high-resolution images of painted surfaces, detailed three-dimensional scans, and metadata annotated by archaeologists. Ground truth comes from years of excavation, cleaning, and manual reconstruction. Archaeologists assembled a subset of approximately 1,000 pieces from roughly 16,000 available fragments, and all fragments were digitized in three dimensions.

The benchmark uses this material to assess current computational and data-driven reassembly methods. Tested baselines reveal a clear gap in solving the real reconstruction problem. The dataset’s importance lies in making archaeological damage and incomplete evidence part of the evaluation itself. Methods must contend with the visual and geometric irregularities found in actual fragments, rather than succeeding only under the cleaner conditions of synthetic puzzle construction.
neurips-2024-re-assembling-the-past-the-.tldr: RePAIR benchmarks real-world reassembly using damaged fresco fragments, multimodal scans, and archaeologist-established partial ground truth.

paragraphs: Neural network verification can use cutting planes, or cuts, to narrow the search involved in proving a property. Existing cutting-plane approaches such as GCP-CROWN depend on generic cuts from external mixed-integer programming solvers. Those solvers scale poorly, preventing large networks from benefiting from the same technique.

BICCOS generates cuts using the structure of neural network verification itself. It examines logical relationships among neurons in subproblems already verified during branch-and-bound search, then introduces constraints that exclude those relationships in other subproblems. Influence scores assigned to neurons along search paths help strengthen the resulting cuts. A multi-tree search finds additional cuts and further reduces the search space.

The experiments show that BICCOS generates hundreds of useful cuts during verification and consistently increases the number of instances verified relative to other state-of-the-art verifiers across the tested benchmarks. This includes large networks beyond the reach of earlier cutting-plane methods. The contribution is a way to reuse information discovered during verification, turning completed subproblems into constraints that accelerate the remaining search.
neurips-2024-scalable-neural-network-ver.tldr: BICCOS derives verification-specific cutting planes from branch-and-bound search, enabling more instances and larger networks to be verified.

paragraphs: Speech recognizers need to adapt to target conditions such as unfamiliar accents and noise, but labeled recordings may be unavailable. Self-TAught Recognizer, or STAR, adapts speech foundation models using unlabeled audio. It targets Transformer-related models with autoregressive decoding, including Whisper and Canary.

The key component is an indicator that assesses the quality of individual tokens in automatically generated transcripts without access to correct transcripts. It combines information produced step by step during decoding and uses that assessment to guide model updates. This gives adaptation a way to distinguish more useful pseudo-label information from less reliable information within the same generated output.

Across 14 target domains, STAR achieves an average 13.5% relative reduction in word error rate and sometimes approaches supervised adaptation performance. The authors also observe avoidance of catastrophic forgetting without revisiting source-domain data. Experiments report effectiveness with less than one hour of unlabeled data and applicability to other large speech models and speech translation. These findings support quality-aware pseudo-labeling as a practical route to efficient unsupervised adaptation.
neurips-2024-self-taught-recognizer-towa.tldr: STAR uses decoding-based token quality estimates to adapt speech models from unlabeled audio, reducing word error rates across diverse target domains.

paragraphs: Molecular representations benefit from three-dimensional geometry because spatial structure carries information about physicochemical properties. Diffusion models have shown promise in generating molecular conformations, but the paper identifies a weakness in many existing approaches: they treat atoms as independent entities and overlook dependencies within molecular substructures.

SubgDiff incorporates molecular subgraphs into the diffusion framework to make the denoising network more aware of those substructures. It introduces three components: subgraph prediction, an expectation state, and k-step diffusion using the same subgraph. Together, these are intended to make grouped molecular structure part of what the model learns during denoising, rather than leaving the representation centered on individual atoms.

The authors evaluate the learned representations on extensive downstream tasks and report superior performance, especially for molecular force prediction. This connects the diffusion design to the usefulness of the resulting molecular features, beyond conformation generation alone. The findings support incorporating dependencies among atoms within substructures as a way to improve representations for subsequent molecular prediction tasks.
neurips-2024-subgdiff-a-subgraph-diffusi.tldr: SubgDiff incorporates molecular subgraphs into diffusion training to improve molecular representations, with particularly strong reported results for force prediction.

paragraphs: Image-guided 3D generation can produce convincing appearances while leaving the underlying surface too smooth. It can also encode apparent geometric detail in surface color instead of actual geometry. Tactile DreamFusion introduces touch information to help generated assets contain realistic fine surface structure as well as plausible visual appearance.

The method uses a lightweight 3D texture field guided by diffusion priors from both visual and tactile domains. High-resolution tactile normals condition visual texture generation, linking appearance to detailed surface orientation. A customized TextureDreambooth guides tactile refinement on local patches, and a multi-part pipeline allows different regions of an object to receive different textures.

The authors evaluate the approach for both text-to-3D and image-to-3D generation. Their experiments report realistic, customizable fine geometric textures while maintaining alignment between visual and tactile modalities. The significance is that touch contributes information about surface structure that visual generation alone may represent inadequately. The combined system aims to make the generated asset’s appearance and geometric texture agree, including when different regions require different surface treatments.
neurips-2024-tactile-dreamfusion-exploit.tldr: Tactile DreamFusion combines visual and touch-based diffusion guidance to generate finer, mutually aligned surface geometry and appearance.

paragraphs: A conventional language model scores or generates a response from a query. This paper investigates the reverse relationship: scoring or generating the query given a response. Time Reversed Language Models use that direction to provide unsupervised feedback that can complement the predictions of a forward model.

The authors train TRLM-Ba from scratch with reversed token order during pretraining and fine-tuning. They use reverse scores to rerank candidate responses generated by forward models, supported by empirical evidence and theory in a stylized setting. On AlpacaEval, the approach achieves up to 5% improvement over best-of-N selection using self log-perplexity scores, and reverse scoring also yields gains in citation generation and passage retrieval.

The models’ ability to generate queries provides another application: augmenting or supplying feedback to input safety filters. Against several JailbreakBench attacks, this substantially reduces false negatives while having negligible effects on false positives. The findings show that reversing the conditioning direction can supply useful evaluation and safety signals, rather than relying exclusively on how likely a response is given its prompt.
neurips-2024-time-reversal-provides-unsu.tldr: Time-reversed language models score and generate queries from responses, providing useful feedback for response selection, retrieval, and safety filtering.

paragraphs: Many useful data collections consist of images, conversations, or reviews rather than neatly structured tables. UQE investigates how language models can support analytics directly over these collections. Its goal is to combine the expressive semantic interpretation of foundation models with the organized execution of a database query engine.

Users write requests in Universal Query Language, a SQL dialect whose conditions and operators can be expressed flexibly in natural language. The engine uses language models to interpret unstructured content, while sampling and optimization techniques support efficient, accurate execution. It also applies ideas from compiler theory to coordinate sampling operations and foundation-model calls within the query workflow.

The paper demonstrates the engine across images, dialogs, and reviews, with tasks including conditional aggregation, semantic retrieval, and abstraction aggregation. These demonstrations establish the usefulness of coordinating model-based analysis through a query system. The contribution lies in connecting a flexible interface for asking questions with an execution strategy that manages how unstructured data is sampled and analyzed, rather than treating each model call as an isolated operation.
neurips-2024-uqe-a-query-engine-for-unst.tldr: UQE combines a natural-language-flexible SQL dialect with model calls, sampling, and optimization to analyze unstructured data collections.

paragraphs: Text-to-video diffusion models can struggle with complex scenes containing several objects or changing numbers of objects over time. Longer videos make this harder because the generated sequence must follow evolving textual instructions while remaining coherent. VideoTetris addresses these challenges through compositional control over video generation.

Its central mechanism manipulates and combines attention maps within denoising networks across both space and time. This gives the generation process a way to organize different parts of the textual description according to where and when they should influence the video. The framework also adds a data-processing pipeline that accounts for dynamics and a consistency regularizer for autoregressive generation.

The experiments report strong qualitative and quantitative results for compositional text-to-video generation. The components address related but distinct needs: attention composition supports complex textual semantics, while the processing pipeline and regularizer improve consistency as generation proceeds. Together, they offer a framework for handling videos whose content changes over time, including scenes where object composition is more complicated than a single persistent subject.
neurips-2024-videotetris-towards-composi.tldr: VideoTetris composes attention across space and time to generate complex videos while improving consistency during autoregressive generation.

paragraphs: Asynchronous distributed learning allows workers to operate independently and send updates intermittently. This supports heterogeneous computing resources, but delayed updates introduce bias and complicate the detection of harmful contributions. Byzantine failures, which include malicious or erroneous worker behavior, therefore interact with the timing differences already present in the system.

The paper introduces weighted robust aggregation tailored to these asynchronous dynamics. It extends robust aggregators and a recent meta-aggregator into weighted forms to mitigate the effects of delayed updates. This makes update timing part of the aggregation framework used to preserve learning integrity, rather than treating robustness and asynchronous execution as separate concerns.

The authors combine this framework with a recent variance-reduction technique and establish an optimal convergence rate in the asynchronous Byzantine setting they study. They support the method with both theoretical and empirical analysis. The contribution connects fault tolerance with efficient learning: weighting handles the complications introduced by delayed updates, while variance reduction helps obtain the stated convergence result in the presence of disruptive workers.
neurips-2024-weight-for-robustness-a-com.tldr: Weighted robust aggregation and variance reduction enable an optimal convergence rate in the paper’s asynchronous Byzantine learning setting.
